draft.title: Measuring physical activity
card: Questionnaire
people answer set questions about what they did, often over a past week. It is cheap and suits large groups, but people may forget or overstate how active they were.
Diary
a person records activity as it happens or soon after. It gives detail on type and time, but it takes effort to keep up and relies on honest entries.
Pedometer
a small device, often worn at the hip, that counts steps. It is cheap and simple, but it does not show intensity and misses activities such as cycling or swimming.
Heart rate monitor
a device that records heart rate, which shows how hard the body is working. It is useful for intensity, but heart rate can also rise from stress, heat or caffeine.
draft.remember: Self-reports are cheap but rely on memory and honesty. Devices record data directly but each has limits.

a.q: A researcher wants to measure the activity of 2000 students cheaply. Which method suits this best, and what is its main limit?
opts: Questionnaire, because students may overstate their activity
Heart rate monitor, because students may overstate activity
Questionnaire, because it cannot be given to large groups
Heart rate monitor, because it only counts steps taken
a.why: A questionnaire is cheap and works for large groups, but it depends on what students remember and report. A heart rate monitor records data directly, but it is a poorer fit for 2000 students, and it does not count steps.
a.clue: Think about cost and group size.

b.q: Sam wants to know how hard his body worked during a netball game, not just how much he moved. Which method best shows this, and what limit applies?
opts: Heart rate monitor, as heart rate can rise from heat
Pedometer, as it shows intensity but costs a lot
Diary, as it records intensity but is hard to keep up
Pedometer, as heart rate can rise from heat or stress
b.why: A heart rate monitor shows how hard the body is working, so it suits intensity. Its limit is that heart rate can also rise for reasons other than exercise. A pedometer only counts steps and does not show intensity.
b.clue: Which device tracks effort, not just steps?

proposal.title: Measuring physical activity
card: Self-report

questionnaires ask about past activity and are a cheap way to survey large groups, while diaries record activity as it happens but take effort to keep. Both rely on memory and honesty, so people may overstate how active they were.
Pedometer
a cheap, simple device, often worn at the hip, that counts steps. It does not show intensity and misses activities such as cycling or swimming.
Accelerometer
a small device that measures movement in several directions, so it can show both the amount and the intensity of movement. It is more accurate than a pedometer but costs more.
Heart rate monitor
a device that records heart rate, which shows how hard the body is working. It is useful for intensity, but heart rate can also rise from stress, heat or caffeine.
proposal.remember: Self-reports are cheap but rely on memory and honesty. Devices record data directly, but each has its own limits.

a.q: A researcher wants to measure the activity of 2000 students cheaply. Which method suits this best, and what is its main limit?
opts: Questionnaire; limit: students may overstate activity
Accelerometer; limit: students may overstate activity
Questionnaire; limit: it cannot be used with large groups
Heart rate monitor; limit: it only counts steps taken
a.why: A questionnaire is cheap and suits large groups, but it relies on what students remember and choose to report. An accelerometer records movement directly, so overstating is not its limit, and its higher cost makes it a poor fit for 2000 students.
a.clue: Think about cost and group size, then about who supplies the data.

b.q: Sam wants to know how hard his body worked during a netball game, not just how much he moved. Which method best shows this, and what limit applies?
opts: Heart rate monitor; limit: heat can also raise heart rate
Pedometer; limit: it misses cycling and swimming
Diary; limit: it takes effort to keep up each day
Heart rate monitor; limit: it only counts steps taken
b.why: A heart rate monitor shows how hard the body is working, and its limit is that heart rate can also rise from heat, stress or caffeine. The pedometer limit is real, but a pedometer only counts steps and cannot show how hard Sam worked.
b.clue: Which device tracks the body's effort, and what else can change its reading?
